text: Around the same time, another New Deal agency drew the idea onto maps.
The Home Owners Loan Corporation had been set up to refinance failing mortgages.
From 1935 to 1940 it surveyed two hundred and thirty nine American cities and graded them block by block in color.
Green was A, the best.
Blue was B.
Yellow was C.
Red was D, hazardous, the lowest grade.
The notes the surveyors wrote down explain the colors.
A green area was native born and well off.
A red area was old, crowded, or, again and again in the margins, home to Negro families or what one surveyor called an infiltration of them.
On the Chicago maps, the Black Belt on the South Side was washed in red.
The grade was not really about the houses.
It was about who lived inside them.
The word redlining comes from that red ink.
A family in a red zone could not get a federally backed loan no matter how steady their paycheck was.
They could not buy.
They often could not borrow to repair.
So the houses aged, and rents stayed high because there was nowhere else to go, and absentee landlords carved single homes into a dozen kitchenettes.
Then a new surveyor would arrive, see the crowding the redline had caused, and grade the block hazardous all over again.
The map became a wall, and the wall became real.
